title: Averages, Medians, and Data Traps
description: Learn to avoid common statistical pitfalls when interpreting business metrics like averages, medians, and correlations.

interactions.prompt: A startup's 10 employees earn $50K each, but the CEO earns $950K. Which metric best represents a typical salary?

options.text: Mean ($130K), because it includes all earners
Median ($50K), because it resists the CEO outlier
Mode ($50K), but only because the sample is small
Range ($900K), because it shows full spread

interactions.teachingPreamble: The average (mean) adds everything up and divides equally, but a single extreme value can distort it dramatically. The median is the middle value when you line up all numbers  -  it's far more resistant to outliers, making it the go-to metric when data is skewed.

interactions.prompt: Shopify reports that its merchants' mean monthly revenue is $12,400 but median monthly revenue is $2,100. What does this gap tell you?

options.text: Most merchants earn close to $12,400
A small number of high-revenue merchants skew the mean upward
The data was collected incorrectly
Revenue is evenly distributed across merchants

interactions.prompt: Cities with more ice cream shops also have higher crime rates. What should you conclude?

options.text: Ice cream shops cause crime
Crime causes ice cream shops to open
A third factor like population size likely drives both
The correlation must be a data error

interactions.teachingPreamble: Correlation means two things move together, but causation means one actually causes the other. In business, confusing the two leads to costly mistakes  -  like assuming a marketing campaign drove sales when a seasonal trend was the real driver. Always ask: could a hidden third variable explain both?

interactions.prompt: When a dataset has extreme outliers pulling the mean away from most values, the distribution is said to be ____.

options.text: Normal
Skewed
Correlated
Randomized

interactions.prompt: Your DTC brand tested a new homepage. Version B showed a 15% conversion lift, but only 80 visitors were in the test. Do you ship the change or keep testing?

options.text: Ship it  -  a 15% lift is too big to ignore
Keep testing  -  80 visitors is far too small to trust
Ship it but monitor results closely for a week
Discard the test entirely and redesign from scratch

interactions.prompt: Netflix surveys 50 users and finds 80% love a new feature. Should they confidently roll it out to 230 million subscribers?

options.text: Yes  -  80% approval is overwhelmingly positive
No  -  50 users can't reliably represent 230 million
Yes  -  surveys are always representative of the population
No  -  they should only use internal employee feedback

interactions.teachingPreamble: Sample size determines how trustworthy your findings are. A small sample can produce dramatic-looking results purely by chance. As a rule of thumb, larger and more representative samples give you more confidence that your results reflect reality  -  not random noise.

interactions.prompt: Your team is evaluating whether a pricing change boosted revenue. Rank these checks from most to least important for trusting the result.

options.text: Check if the sample size was large enough
Confirm no other changes happened during the test period
Verify if mean or median revenue is being reported
Look at the visual design of the chart used

interactions.prompt: You now learn the pricing test ran during Black Friday week. With this new context, what's your biggest concern about the revenue increase?

options.text: The seasonal spike makes it impossible to isolate the pricing effect
Black Friday customers are more price-sensitive than average
The sample size was probably too small during a holiday
Revenue always goes up in Q4 regardless of pricing

interactions.priorContext: Previously, your team was evaluating whether a pricing change boosted revenue and confirmed the sample size and metric type. Now you discover the test ran during Black Friday week  -  a major confounding variable.
